title: Synergistic Graphene and PEDOT:PSS Layers on Silicon for Enhanced Efficiency and Stability in Schottky Junction Solar Cells
authors: Kentaro Nakajo, Hojun Im, Keiichiro Nishimura, Masahiro Teraoka, Masaya Kikuchi
abstract: While graphene/n-type silicon (Gr/n-Si) and PEDOT:PSS/n-Si solar cells offer a cost-effective alternative to conventional photovoltaics, achieving simultaneous high power conversion efficiency (PCE) and long-term environmental stability remains a formidable challenge. Here, we report the synergistic enhancement of both performance and stability in a planar trilayer PEDOT:PSS/Gr/n-Si Schottky junction architecture. By systematically benchmarking this hybrid device against pristine Gr/n-Si and PEDOT:PSS/n-Si reference cells fabricated on untextured substrates, we isolate the fundamental optoelectronic and barrier functions of the carbon lattice. Comprehensive analyses reveal that the PEDOT:PSS layer simultaneously functions as an anti-reflection coating, a moderate p-type dopant for the underlying graphene, and a conductivity enhancer, collectively optimizing interfacial charge transport. Consequently, the trilayer device achieves a PCE of 8.52%, markedly outperforming the pristine Gr/n-Si reference cell (4.56%). Crucially, the atomic impermeability of the graphene sheet serves as a robust environmental barrier. While bare PEDOT:PSS/n-Si junctions retained only ~29% of their initial efficiency after 75 days of ambient exposure, graphene shields the active junction from moisture-induced degradation of the hygroscopic PEDOT:PSS overlayer. This enables the trilayer device to retain approximately 90% of its initial efficiency over the same 75-day period. The complementary roles of graphene as both a highly crystalline charge transport interface and an impermeable protective barrier establish a highly effective strategy for engineering high-efficiency, environmentally stable hybrid photovoltaics.

infographic.key_insight: A PEDOT:PSS/graphene/n-Si trilayer improves solar-cell efficiency while using graphene to protect the junction against environmental degradation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The planar architecture combines optical, electrical, and protective functions to improve the performance and durability of hybrid silicon photovoltaics.

infographic.evidence_signal: The trilayer achieved 8.52% efficiency versus 4.56% for graphene/n-Si and retained approximately 90% of its initial efficiency after 75 days, versus approximately 29% for PEDOT:PSS/n-Si.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish durability beyond 75 days or the scalability of producing defect-free graphene barriers.
infographic.paper_title: Synergistic Graphene and PEDOT:PSS Layers on Silicon for Enhanced Efficiency and Stability in Schottky Junction Solar Cells

title: Evidence-grounded large language models guide perovskite solar cell design and optimization
authors: YanKai Chen, Zhi Wan, ZiHao Li, Tao Jing
abstract: Using large language models to interpret experimental evidence, design discriminating experiments and formulate well-supported mechanistic explanations remains a central challenge in materials research. Here we establish PSM-Bench, an 800-question benchmark developed by perovskite researchers to evaluate scientific reasoning in perovskite photovoltaics. We also introduce OpenPerov, an expert-informed language-model framework that learns from expert-calibrated evidence records reconstructed from 4,035 training articles; these records link experimental strategies, controls and observations to mechanistic interpretations. Structured-evidence adaptation outperformed conventional question-answer training, and OpenPerov Flash ranked first among 13 closed-book systems. OpenPerov Pro raised Scientific Mastery further, from 87.6 to 89.1, by revising selected passages with retrieved evidence. On questions derived from subsequent studies, both models also outscored expert-authored answers. In an experimental test of self-assembled monolayer design, OpenPerov selected a K analogue that outperformed the Na analogue preferred by experts. Devices incorporating the selected contact reached a power conversion efficiency of 27.05% and retained 96.74% of their initial efficiency after 1,000 h of dark thermal ageing at 85 $^\circ$C. These results show that reconstructed scientific reasoning provides an effective basis for building domain models that interpret experiments and inform materials design.

infographic.key_insight: Evidence-trained language models guided perovskite contact design, selecting a K analogue that outperformed the expert-preferred Na analogue.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Devices using the AI-selected contact achieved 27.05% power conversion efficiency and retained 96.74% of initial efficiency after 1,000 hours of dark thermal ageing at 85°C.
method: Reconstruct expert-calibrated evidence records from 4,035 training articles.

infographic.paper_title: Evidence-grounded large language models guide perovskite solar cell design and optimization

title: Multiwavelength Photoluminescence as a Non-destructive Probe of Depth-Dependent UV Damage in Perovskite Semiconductors
authors: Zixu Huang, Julisa Juarez, Akash Dasgupta, David S. Ginger
abstract: Buried interfaces play a critical role in the operational stability of perovskite optoelectronic devices, yet remain challenging to probe non-destructively. Here, we demonstrate a multiwavelength photoluminescence-based approach exploiting the wavelength-dependent absorption of perovskites, enabling fast, and non-destructive probing of depth-sensitive degradation behavior of perovskite devices under operational conditions. Using ultraviolet (UV) light-soaking with different indium tin oxide (ITO) modifiers as a test case, we employ wide-field photoluminescence (PL) imaging, time-resolved photoluminescence (trPL) and ideality factor measurements with different wavelength excitation to characterize degradation behavior of both perovskite thin films and photovoltaic devices under UV soaking. Using only nondestructive characterization, we show that UV-induced degradation in p-i-n perovskite solar cells occurs preferentially at the HTL interface, adversely affecting device stability, consistent with ex-situ destructive tests. Our results also show that modifying the buried interface with 3-mercaptopropyltrimethoxysilane reduces UV-induced damage at the buried interface, thus improving the UV stability of both perovskite films and devices. This work establishes a fast, non-destructive strategy to screen depth-dependent degradation in perovskite devices, offering insights for interface design and stability optimization.

infographic.key_insight: Multiwavelength photoluminescence non-destructively reveals depth-dependent UV damage in perovskite solar cells, identifying preferential degradation at the buried hole-transport-layer interface.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Depth-sensitive optical screening can guide buried-interface design, with 3-mercaptopropyltrimethoxysilane modification improving UV stability in perovskite films and devices.
method: Use wavelength-dependent absorption to probe different depths with photoluminescence excitation.
Combine wide-field PL imaging, time-resolved PL, and ideality-factor measurements during UV-soaking studies.

infographic.evidence_signal: Non-destructive measurements localized UV degradation to the buried interface, consistent with ex-situ destructive tests, and showed reduced damage after interface modification.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports no quantitative stability gains, and UV-soaking results alone do not establish durability under broader operating conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Multiwavelength Photoluminescence as a Non-destructive Probe of Depth-Dependent UV Damage in Perovskite Semiconductors

title: Provenance-grouped protocol for evaluating machine learning in perovskite photovoltaics
authors: Qiwei Han, Chi Zhou
abstract: Machine-learning models for perovskite solar cells are typically evaluated using random data splits, which we show systematically leak information through massive internal duplication. Because nearly two-thirds of curated devices share their exact recipe with another, random splits primarily reward the mere recall of historical data rather than testing true physical generalisation. To solve this, we mapped the institutional provenance of the Perovskite Database and established a rigorous hierarchy of grouped splits that progressively isolate duplicate devices, publications, and institutions. Benchmarking thirteen models establishes new state-of-the-art performance across all splits and reveals a critical regime shift: while tree ensembles dominate random splits by recognising familiar recipes, their ranking collapses on genuinely unseen institutions and future discoveries, where composition-aware neural architectures excel. Furthermore, feature importance demonstrates that the device architecture and fabrication methodology dictate final efficiency just as strongly as the absorber chemistry. This standardised protocol empowers the community to separate memorisation from true physical discovery.

infographic.key_insight: Random splits can reward recipe memorisation in perovskite solar-cell models, while provenance-grouped evaluation better tests generalisation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Evaluating on unseen institutions and future discoveries can help identify models better suited to guiding new solar-cell experiments.
method: Map institutional provenance in the Perovskite Database.
Use hierarchical grouped splits to isolate duplicate devices, publications and institutions.
Benchmark 13 models and analyse feature importance.
infographic.evidence_signal: Nearly two-thirds of curated devices share an exact recipe with another; tree ensembles lead on random splits, but composition-aware neural models excel on unseen institutions and future discoveries.
infographic.watch_item: Reliable implementation depends on accurate recipe matching and publication-to-institution provenance mapping.
infographic.paper_title: Provenance-grouped protocol for evaluating machine learning in perovskite photovoltaics

title: Controlling Surface Chemistry in Tin-Lead Perovskites for High-Efficiency Solar Cells
authors: Lijun Chen, Sitong Zhao, Gaukhar Nigmetova, David Garcia Romero, Matteo Pitaro, Sofia Lerda
abstract: Interfacial nonradiative recombination limits tin-lead perovskite photovoltaics. Here we show that neutral ethylenediamine chelates undercoordinated metals at tin-rich surfaces, weakens metal-iodide bonds, and removes excess tin, reconstructing the surface towards a stoichiometric tin-to-lead ratio. In contrast, protonated ethylenediammonium iodide initially passivates undercoordinated metal sites before undergoing defect-assisted deprotonation. Atomistic simulations reveal that subsurface iodide vacancies promote iodide migration and lower the energetic cost of deprotonation. Ethylenediamine-induced reconstruction produces stronger n-type surface character, facilitates electron extraction into C60, and suppresses interfacial nonradiative recombination, enabling methylammonium-free solar cells with a power conversion efficiency of 25.86%. Together, these distinct surface reaction pathways and the defect-assisted evolution of the passivating species underscore the importance of understanding perovskite surface chemistry for the rational design of molecular passivation strategies.

infographic.key_insight: Ethylenediamine reconstructs tin-rich tin–lead perovskite surfaces, improving electron extraction and reducing interfacial losses to enable 25.86% solar-cell efficiency.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Controlling passivant protonation and surface stoichiometry offers a route to more efficient methylammonium-free perovskite solar cells.
method: Compare neutral ethylenediamine with protonated ethylenediammonium iodide surface treatments.
Use atomistic simulations to investigate vacancy-assisted iodide migration and deprotonation.

infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 25.86% power conversion efficiency and simulations showing that subsurface iodide vacancies lower the energetic cost of deprotonation.
infographic.watch_item: Long-term operational stability and scalability of the surface treatment are not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Controlling Surface Chemistry in Tin-Lead Perovskites for High-Efficiency Solar Cells

title: Amorphous selenium-alloyed TeOx thin-film solar cells
authors: Zhaoheng Ling, Linqu Luo, Chrysa Aivalioti, Temur Maksudov, Mengxi Zhang, Theodoulos Kalogerakis
abstract: Tellurium dioxide (TeO$_2$) is a wide-bandgap oxide with attractive processing versatility and emerging p-type semiconducting behaviour, making it a promising material system for optoelectronic and photovoltaic applications. However, TeO$_2$-derived thin films prepared by scalable manufacturing processes, such as vacuum sublimation, can contain residual metallic Te$^0$ species that introduce trap states, limit hole transport, and promote carrier recombination. Here, we demonstrate a selenium alloying strategy to control the defect chemistry of vacuum-sublimed TeO$_x$ films. TeO$_2$:Se powder mixtures (90:10~wt\%) were thermally evaporated and subsequently annealed in air at 225~$^\circ$C for up to 9~h, yielding amorphous TeO$_x$:Se films with an optical bandgap of 0.98~eV under optimised conditions. Structural, chemical, optical, and electrical analyses show that prolonged annealing promotes Se redistribution, suppresses residual Te$^0$ to approximately 0.4\%, reduces the film's surface roughness, and shifts the valence-band edge. To evaluate the potential of TeO$_x$:Se for photovoltaic applications, we fabricated thin-film solar cells with an ITO/ZnO/TeO$_x$:Se/MoO$_x$/Ag architecture. Devices based on an 80~nm TeO$_x$:Se active layer annealed for 9~h exhibit optimal performance, with broadband photocurrent generation from 300 to 1000~nm, yielding an open-circuit voltage of 0.50~V, a short-circuit current density of 8.50~mA~cm$^{-2}$, a fill factor of 0.44, and a maximum power conversion efficiency of approximately 1.87\%. These results establish selenium-alloyed TeO$_x$ as a viable oxide-derived absorber for thin-film photovoltaics and highlight chemical-state control as an effective route for improving photovoltaic performance.

infographic.key_insight: Selenium alloying and air annealing suppress residual metallic tellurium in amorphous TeOx films, enabling thin-film solar cells with approximately 1.87% peak efficiency.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Chemical-state control offers a route to improving oxide-derived photovoltaic absorbers made by scalable vacuum deposition.
method: Thermally evaporate TeO2:Se powder mixtures at a 90:10 weight ratio.

infographic.watch_item: The 9-hour annealing step may constrain manufacturing throughput, and the abstract does not report long-term device stability.
infographic.paper_title: Amorphous selenium-alloyed TeOx thin-film solar cells

title: Stable AgBiS2 near-infrared absorbers for thin film tandem photovoltaics
authors: Shiling Dong, Yongjie Wang, Hae-Jun Seok, Mengyuan Huang, Edward Newton, Der Ying Chen
abstract: AgBiS2 has rapidly risen in efficiency as single-junction photovoltaics (PVs), but its potential for tandem PVs is unexplored. Herein, we perform optical modeling based on the experimental absorption spectrum of AgBiS2, revealing that, as the NIR sub-cell, efficiencies exceeding 47.9% are achievable in triple-junction tandems, superseding tandems using Pb/Sn perovskite NIR cells (35.9%). However, fulfilling this potential requires overcoming the limited transport properties of AgBiS2 nanocrystal films, which constrains film thicknesses to only 30-50 nm, severely restricting NIR response. A solution-phase ligand exchange process is herein developed, allowing one-step deposition of passivated AgBiS2 nanocrystals that maintain efficient charge-carrier extraction despite an order of magnitude increase in film thickness. These films enable 24.0%-efficient four-terminal tandems with visible-light-absorbing lead-halide perovskite sub-cells, and monolithic tandems successfully demonstrating voltage addition. AgBiS2 PVs have high stability, retaining >90% of the original efficiency after 3 months of storage in dry air without encapsulation. This work establishes the significant potential of AgBiS2 as a stable and scalable NIR absorber for tandem PVs.

infographic.key_insight: Solution-phase ligand exchange enables thicker, charge-extracting AgBiS2 nanocrystal films for near-infrared tandem solar cells.
infographic.engineering_relevance: One-step deposition of passivated AgBiS2 offers a route toward scalable near-infrared sub-cells paired with visible-light perovskite absorbers.
method: Model tandem performance using the measured AgBiS2 absorption spectrum.
Use solution-phase ligand exchange to passivate nanocrystals and increase usable film thickness.

infographic.paper_title: Stable AgBiS2 near-infrared absorbers for thin film tandem photovoltaics

title: High-Entropy A-Site Disorder Enhances Oxygen Evolution Reaction Activity and Stability in Nickelate Thin Films
authors: Min-Ju Choi, Le Wang, Krishna Prasad Koirala, Hyoju Park, Mark E. Bowden, Elizabeth Helen Krenkel
abstract: Rare-earth nickelates are among the most active oxide electrocatalysts for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER), owing to their tunable Ni-O covalency, near-unity eg occupancy, and sensitivity to A-site chemistry, oxygen stoichiometry, and epitaxial strain. Here, we use epitaxial A-site high-entropy (La0.2Pr0.2Nd0.2Sm0.2Eu0.2)NiO3 thin films to reveal how epitaxial strain influences defect formation, Ni valence, electronic structure, and OER activity in a chemically disordered rare-earth (RE) sublattice. Tensile strain promotes Ruddlesden-Popper fault formation, interrupts the corner-sharing NiO6 network, and lowers the average Ni oxidation state. Although the occupied density of states near the Fermi level remains largely unchanged, O K-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy reveals increased low-energy unoccupied states under tensile strain. First-principles calculations suggest that tensile strain shifts RE 4f-derived states toward the Fermi level, enhancing RE 4f-O 2p-Ni 3d hybridization. These coupled structural and electronic changes lead to earlier OER onset, stronger pre-catalytic Ni redox features, and higher activity than compressively strained films and representative single-A-site nickelates. The high-entropy nickelate also shows enhanced resistance to OER-induced structural degradation compared with LaNiO3. These results suggest that A-site configurational disorder and epitaxial strain can jointly tune defect formation and rare-earth-derived electronic states, providing a route for improving perovskite oxide electrocatalysts.

infographic.key_insight: A-site high-entropy disorder and tensile epitaxial strain jointly improve nickelate thin-film oxygen evolution activity, with enhanced structural stability relative to LaNiO3.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work offers a materials-design strategy for oxide water-electrolysis catalysts, rather than solar cells or AI systems.
method: Study epitaxial (La0.2Pr0.2Nd0.2Sm0.2Eu0.2)NiO3 films under different strain conditions.

infographic.paper_title: High-Entropy A-Site Disorder Enhances Oxygen Evolution Reaction Activity and Stability in Nickelate Thin Films

title: A Hybrid TFT-NBEATS Framework for Robust Multi-Horizon Photovoltaic Power Forecasting
authors: Shafi Bin Sultan, Sabik Bin Sultan, Mohammad Tajrian Arafat Alvi, Rayhanul Islam Sony, Abdulah Al Numan
abstract: Accurate multi-horizon photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting is essential for grid stability, energy scheduling, and the efficient operation of PVbatterygrid systems. However, existing models often fail to jointly capture short-term variability and long-term temporal patterns, while lacking unified multi-horizon capability and interpretability. To address these limitations, this study proposes a novel hybrid deep learning framework that integrates a Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) and N-BEATS within an attention-based fusion architecture. The proposed model leverages TFT to learn short-term temporal dependencies and dynamic feature importance, while N-BEATS captures long-term trend and seasonal components through interpretable basis decomposition. An adaptive attention mechanism dynamically fuses both branches, enabling balanced multi-scale learning. The framework simultaneously generates forecasts for 30-minute, 2-hour, 6-hour, 12-hour, and 24-hour horizons within a single unified pipeline. The model is evaluated using multi-year real-world datasets from the Desert Knowledge Australia Solar Centre (DKASC). Experimental results demonstrate superior performance over statistical, machine learning, and deep learning baselines. The proposed model achieves RMSE values of 42.35, 46.27, 52.29, and 48.11 across the 20162017, 2023, 2024, and 20252026 datasets, respectively, corresponding to a 3540% reduction compared to the best baseline (TFT). Additionally, MAPE remains below 5% across all datasets, indicating high predictive accuracy and stability. The model also provides interpretability through attention visualization and trendseasonality decomposition, and is deployed on a cloud-based platform for real-time forecasting. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework is robust, interpretable, and suitable for practical renewable energy applications.

infographic.key_insight: A hybrid TFT–N-BEATS model combines short-term dynamics with long-term patterns to forecast PV power across five horizons.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Multi-horizon PV forecasts can support grid stability, energy scheduling, and coordinated PV–battery–grid operation.
method: TFT learns short-term dependencies and dynamic feature importance.

infographic.paper_title: A Hybrid TFT-NBEATS Framework for Robust Multi-Horizon Photovoltaic Power Forecasting

title: The polar discontinuity picture in nickelate superlattices: comparison of the insulating and metallic phases
authors: Edith Simmen, Jonathan Amara, Philippe Ghosez, Nicola A. Spaldin
abstract: We present a first-principles study of the formal-charge polar discontinuity in superlattices of BaTiO$_3$ interfaced with SmNiO$_3$ or BiNiO$_3$, comparing the results for the insulating and metallic nickelate phases. Polar discontinuities arising from differently charged layers in perovskites are well-studied in heterostructures such as LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$, and recently, signatures consistent with such a polar discontinuity have been observed in systems where the formally charged layers would reside in a metal. We first identify signatures of the polar discontinuity in the structure and the density of states of superlattices with BaTiO$_3$ and insulating BiNiO$_3$, and find partial screening by modification of the BiNiO$_3$ charge disproportionation pattern analogous to our previous study on BaTiO$_3$/SmNiO$_3$. We then examine superlattices constructed from the corresponding metallic nickelate phases and find that, despite the presence of screening charges, the qualitative interfacial response is remarkably similar to that of the insulating counterparts. We show that the metallic screening charges have little influence on the apparent formal-charge polar discontinuity and discuss practical limitations of the polar-discontinuity picture when interpreting and quantifying screening at metallic nickelate/ferroelectric interfaces.

infographic.key_insight: BaTiO₃/nickelate superlattices show qualitatively similar interfacial responses in insulating and metallic phases, despite metallic screening charges.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The findings inform electrostatic modeling of nickelate/ferroelectric interfaces, rather than directly demonstrating AI or solar-cell performance.
method: First-principles calculations of BaTiO₃/SmNiO₃ and BaTiO₃/BiNiO₃ superlattices.
Comparison of insulating and metallic nickelate phases.
Analysis of interfacial structure, density of states, and charge disproportionation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Calculations identify partial screening through altered BiNiO₃ charge disproportionation and little influence of metallic screening charges on the apparent formal-charge polar discontinuity.
infographic.watch_item: The formal-charge polar-discontinuity picture has limitations when interpreting and quantifying screening at metallic nickelate/ferroelectric interfaces.
infographic.paper_title: The polar discontinuity picture in nickelate superlattices: comparison of the insulating and metallic phases

title: Zero-Point Renormalization Reshapes the Shift Current: The Role of Electron-Phonon Coupling
authors: Yang Li, Zuzhang Lin, Zhikuan Wang, Chengzhi Wu, Zeyu Jiang, Bing Huang
abstract: Shift current (SC) drives the bulk photovoltaic effect, holding promise for near-instantaneous, low-dissipation photodetection and energy conversion. The current understanding of SC relies primarily on a single-particle picture, in which the SC is determined purely by band dispersion. While many-body effects from directly excited quasiparticles, such as excitons, magnons and phonons, have been explored, the renormalization of electronic states by quantum virtual-phonon coupling --- inherent in essentially all solids and particularly decisive for transport --- remains unaddressed. Here, using first-principles calculations, we identify this missing channel --- band-renormalized shift current (BRSC) --- in monolayer MoS2. We find that the zero-point renormalization alone, without any polarization-carrying photoexcited phonons and with barely any alteration of the band dispersion, dramatically reshapes the SC spectrum: emergent low-energy peaks arise from phonon-assisted optical transitions between momentum-distinct states, with a pronounced redshift of higher-energy features. A mere 1.0% strain sharply tunes the BRSC, whereas raising the temperature enhances it. Our findings overturn the band-structure-only paradigm, establishing electron-phonon coupling as an indispensable ingredient for nonlinear photocurrent and opening a strain-thermal route for engineering next-generation optoelectronic responses.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum virtual-phonon coupling reshapes the predicted shift-current spectrum of monolayer MoS2 even at zero temperature, despite barely changing its band dispersion.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Accounting for electron–phonon coupling could improve nonlinear photocurrent predictions and guide strain- and temperature-based tuning of optoelectronic devices.
method: First-principles calculations for monolayer MoS2.
Include zero-point electron–phonon renormalization of electronic states.
Evaluate shift-current responses to strain and temperature.
infographic.evidence_signal: Calculations predict new low-energy peaks, redshifted higher-energy features, strong tuning under 1.0% strain, and enhanced band-renormalized shift current with increasing temperature.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports computational results for one material, not experimental validation, solar-cell efficiency gains, or AI-based optimization.
infographic.paper_title: Zero-Point Renormalization Reshapes the Shift Current: The Role of Electron-Phonon Coupling

title: Electronic-morphological decoupling in mixed-dimensional halide perovskite heterostructures
authors: Mahmoud Samadpour, Alireza Fathi Beiraghvandi, Kazem Meraji, Tristan Sachsenweger Ballantyne, Fuxiang Ji, Mahdi Mohammadi
abstract: Surface morphology is widely considered an indicator of thin-film quality, with smoother films generally expected to exhibit more uniform optoelectronic properties. Here, we demonstrate that substantial surface evolution does not necessarily lead to increased electronic heterogeneity in mixed-dimensional perovskite heterostructures. We investigate how low-dimensional Ruddlesden-Popper capping layers derived from the sterically hindered 5-tert-butyl-phenanthridinium cation affect the spatial distributions of photoluminescence (PL) characteristics and quasi-Fermi level splitting (QFLS) in 3D perovskites. By combining statistical atomic force microscopy (AFM) analysis with confocal, spatially resolved PL spectroscopy, we correlate surface topography with microscale optoelectronic properties. Although capping increases surface roughness and height asymmetry, it does not increase electronic inhomogeneity. Instead, the heterostructures exhibit enhanced PL, reduced non-radiative recombination, and improved spatial uniformity of radiative QFLS compared with pristine 3D films. Under accelerated aging, this contrast becomes more pronounced: pristine films develop substantial spatial fluctuations in emission and QFLS, whereas capped heterostructures largely preserve their optoelectronic homogeneity. These findings indicate that the low-dimensional capping layer suppresses aging-induced optoelectronic disorder, demonstrating that electronic uniformity can be maintained despite morphological irregularity. This decoupling provides a design principle for developing durable, high-performance perovskite photovoltaics.

infographic.key_insight: Low-dimensional perovskite capping increases surface roughness while preserving electronic uniformity and suppressing aging-induced optoelectronic disorder.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Surface smoothness alone may be a poor quality metric when designing durable perovskite photovoltaics with electronically protective capping layers.
method: Form mixed-dimensional heterostructures using 5-tert-butyl-phenanthridinium-derived Ruddlesden–Popper capping layers.
Combine statistical AFM with spatially resolved confocal photoluminescence spectroscopy.
Compare morphology, emission, and quasi-Fermi level splitting before and after accelerated aging.
infographic.evidence_signal: Despite greater roughness and height asymmetry, capped films showed enhanced photoluminescence, reduced non-radiative recombination, and more spatially uniform radiative quasi-Fermi level splitting, largely retaining optoelectronic homogeneity during aging.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report device efficiency, quantitative effect sizes, or aging conditions, limiting assessment of practical photovoltaic durability.
infographic.paper_title: Electronic-morphological decoupling in mixed-dimensional halide perovskite heterostructures

title: Impact of organic spacer cations on the light and thermal stability of two-dimensional lead halide perovskites
authors: Mahesh Eledath-Changarath, Jesús Ortiga-Fibla, Andrés F. Gualdrón-Reyes, Jesús Rodríguez-Romero, Iván Mora-Seró, Ana Cros
abstract: Long-term stability remains a critical challenge limiting the photovoltaic and optoelectronic applications of two-dimensional lead halide perovskites. In these materials, the choice of the organic spacer plays a key role not only in enhancing environmental stability, but also in determining their structural characteristics and carrier dynamics. Here, we present an environmental photo- and thermal-stability analysis of BA2PbI4 and PEA2PbI4 two-dimensional lead halide perovskites by means of confocal micro-Raman and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy techniques. We have investigated two different organic spacers, n-butylammonium (BA) and 2-phenylethylammonium (PEA), which provide comparable room-temperature luminescence in freshly exfoliated perovskite nanoflakes and degrade similarly through the removal of organic components and fast crystal phase decomposition into PbI2 and Pb0. However, we observed that the PEA organic cation significantly improves crystal morphology and suppresses lattice defects, resulting in slower degradation and enhanced resistance to light and thermal stress under ambient conditions. Our findings indicate that structural and chemical engineering, along with surface passivation and encapsulation strategies, are essential for achieving long-term stability in two-dimensional halide perovskite devices. Nevertheless, optimizing the balance between stability and device performance remains a critical consideration.

infographic.key_insight: PEA spacers improve crystal morphology and suppress lattice defects, making PEA2PbI4 more resistant to ambient light and thermal degradation than BA2PbI4.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Spacer selection is a useful stability lever for two-dimensional perovskite devices, alongside structural engineering, surface passivation and encapsulation.
method: Compared n-butylammonium (BA) and 2-phenylethylammonium (PEA) spacers.
Evaluated ambient photo- and thermal stability using confocal micro-Raman spectroscopy.
Probed chemical degradation using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy.
infographic.evidence_signal: Freshly exfoliated nanoflakes showed comparable room-temperature luminescence, but PEA-based crystals degraded more slowly despite sharing organic-loss and PbI2/Pb0 decomposition pathways with BA-based crystals.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative stability gains or device-efficiency measurements, so improved material stability should not be equated with demonstrated solar-cell performance.

title: Unifying Low-Frequency Raman and Infrared Signatures across Perovskites
authors: Ethan Berger, Erik Fransson, Apinya Ngoipala, Lucas Svensson, Priyanka Deswal, Mehmet Baskurt
abstract: Perovskites have been studied for a wide range of applications, from oxide-based ferroelectrics to halide-perovskite photovoltaics. Despite their diverse functionalities, these materials share strong lattice anharmonicity arising from structural instabilities such as polar off-centering and octahedral tilting. These anharmonic distortions strongly influence the low-frequency vibrational response and can be observed in infrared (IR) and Raman spectra. However, low-frequency IR and Raman signatures are typically investigated separately, hindering the development of a unified understanding of vibrational spectroscopy across perovskite classes. In this work, we use machine-learning-based molecular dynamics to simulate the IR and Raman spectra of oxide perovskites (SrTiO$_3$ and BaTiO$_3$), halide perovskites (CsPbBr$_3$, CsSnBr$_3$, and CsGeBr$_3$) and double halide perovskites (Cs$_2$AgAlBr$_6$ and Cs$_2$AgBiBr$_6$). By comparing materials exhibiting polar, tilt-driven and mixed instabilities, we find that polar off-centering leads to enhanced low-frequency IR and dielectric responses, whereas nonpolar modes, particularly octahedral tilting, are associated with Raman central peaks. The strength of the low-frequency features also depends on how strongly the underlying modes couple to polarization or dielectric susceptibility. Finally, we show that the dynamics of these instabilities play an important role, with slow polar reorientations shifting the dielectric response to very low frequencies and overdamped tilting modes producing persistent Raman central peaks. These results establish a unified framework connecting low-frequency IR and Raman spectra to the symmetry, coupling and dynamics of their underlying anharmonic lattice instabilities.

infographic.key_insight: Across perovskites, polar off-centering enhances low-frequency infrared and dielectric responses, while nonpolar octahedral tilting is associated with Raman central peaks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Linking spectral signatures to lattice instabilities can help interpret structural dynamics in halide-perovskite solar-cell materials.
method: Use machine-learning-based molecular dynamics to simulate infrared and Raman spectra.
Compare seven oxide, halide and double-halide perovskites with polar, tilt-driven and mixed instabilities.
Relate low-frequency features to mode symmetry, coupling strength and dynamics.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations across seven compositions indicate that slow polar reorientations shift dielectric responses to very low frequencies, while overdamped tilting produces persistent Raman central peaks.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports simulated spectroscopy, not solar-cell performance gains or quantitative experimental validation.
infographic.paper_title: Unifying Low-Frequency Raman and Infrared Signatures across Perovskites

title: Benchmark for Structured Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Perovskite Photovoltaics
authors: Qiwei Han, Chi Zhou, Gaoxiang Yuan
abstract: While retrieval-augmented language models increasingly serve as literature assistants in the physical sciences, existing benchmarks evaluate them primarily on qualitative text overlap or through model-based scoring rather than against verified experimental ground truth. In experimental materials disciplines such as perovskite photovoltaics, however, the most critical inquiries are inherently quantitative and aggregate measurements across dozens or hundreds of papers. Here, we present a quantitative question-answering benchmark where all 755 ground-truth answers are computed directly from 45,441 measured device records (40,889 human-curated records through 2021 and 4,552 records extracted from 2022-2026 literature). Benchmarking six retrieval architectures over 158,274 passages from 25,662 papers using an open 14B model on a single 24 GB GPU, standard passage retrieval tops out at 16-23% accuracy (compared to 1.6-6.5% zero-shot). In contrast, equipping the language model with read-only SQL execution over the structured device table elevates accuracy to 51.5% on historical and 50.8% on prospective literature -- a 33.01.8 percentage-point advantage over hybrid text retrieval. Aggregate queries spanning extrema, distributions, and filtered record counts prove virtually unsolvable via text retrieval alone, demonstrating that systematic table extraction is an operational prerequisite for literature-scale quantitative inquiry.

infographic.key_insight: Read-only SQL access to structured device records raised quantitative question-answering accuracy to about 51%, versus 16–23% for standard passage retrieval.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reliable literature-scale analysis of perovskite solar cells requires structured experimental data, not just retrieval of relevant text.
method: Computed 755 ground-truth answers from 45,441 measured device records.
Benchmarked six retrieval architectures across 158,274 passages from 25,662 papers.
Equipped an open 14B model with read-only SQL access on a single 24 GB GPU.
infographic.evidence_signal: SQL-enabled accuracy reached 51.5% on historical literature and 50.8% on prospective literature; zero-shot accuracy was 1.6–6.5%.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy remained near 51% even with SQL access, so quantitative outputs still require validation.
infographic.paper_title: Benchmark for Structured Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Perovskite Photovoltaics

title: Controlling nitrogen incorporation in (Eu,Ba,Ca)TiO$_3$-derived perovskite-type oxynitrides through Fermi Level Engineering
authors: Margarida Barroso, Marie Neumann, Rachele Sciotto, Shama Perween, Magdalena O. Cichocka, Jefferson Bettini
abstract: Defect states directly influence not only functional properties, but also oxynitride formation during ammonolysis. Along with structural stability and charge balance, these defects can cause non-uniform nitrogen incorporation. To address this, the recently proposed Fermi Level Engineering concept provides a powerful alternative of rationalising oxynitride synthesis. By using the electron chemical potential, i.e., the Fermi level, as a unique descriptor, this approach can predict, understand, and manipulate defect formation enthalpies and charge transition levels, subsequently allowing to incorporate defect-property correlations to the concept. This work combines theoretical modelling and experimental characterisation of barium titanium oxynitrides to explain an intrinsic, self-limiting nitridation process. Progressive nitrogen incorporation causes a Fermi level downward shift, leaving further nitrogen substitution on oxygen sites energetically unfavourable, up to 0.03 N per unit formula. We demonstrate that A-site cation substitution in Eu$_{1-x}$Ba$_x$TiO$_3$- and Eu$_{1-x}$Ca$_x$TiO$_3$-derived oxynitrides can be applied to control compensation of the additional negative charge from N$^{3-}$ and keep the Fermi level high. The Eu$^{2+/3+}$ redox couple enables substitution of oxygen by nitrogen through pinning of the Fermi level at the europium charge transition level, at $\sim$ 2.9 eV above the VBM. This allows for higher nitrogen uptake of up to 0.65 per formula unit (taken from hot gas extraction) through a more controlled process. Further incorporation is then limited by an intra-Ti(O,N)$_6$ octahedra distortion due to internal bond-angle variance. These findings demonstrate that Fermi Level Engineering provides a pathway to predict and overcome intrinsic synthetic and thermodynamic limitations in oxynitride synthesis.

infographic.key_insight: Eu²⁺/Eu³⁺ redox chemistry pins the Fermi level, overcoming self-limiting nitrogen incorporation in perovskite-type oxynitrides.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Fermi-level engineering offers a strategy for controlling oxynitride composition during synthesis, although solar-cell performance is not evaluated here.
method: Combine theoretical modelling with experimental characterisation of titanium oxynitrides.
Tune A-site composition in Eu–Ba and Eu–Ca perovskite-derived oxynitrides.
Use defect energetics and charge compensation to explain nitrogen uptake.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports nitrogen uptake up to 0.03 per formula unit in barium titanium oxynitrides versus up to 0.65 in Eu-containing compositions by hot gas extraction, with Fermi-level pinning approximately 2.9 eV above the valence-band maximum.
infographic.watch_item: Further nitrogen incorporation remains limited by bond-angle distortion within Ti(O,N)₆ octahedra.
infographic.paper_title: Controlling nitrogen incorporation in (Eu,Ba,Ca)TiO$_3$-derived perovskite-type oxynitrides through Fermi Level Engineering

title: PING: physics informed graph neural network for advection-diffusion processes with applications to solar power forecasting
authors: Jelena Simeunović, Baptiste Schubnel, Pierre-Jean Alet, Pascal Frossard, Rafael E. Carrillo
abstract: Advection-diffusion plays an essential role in transport phenomena such as atmospheric and cloud dynamics. Improved forecasting of cloud motion, in turn, enhances solar power production forecasts and facilitates the integration of additional photovoltaic (PV) sources into the power grid. However, both classical numerical models and emerging deep learning approaches face challenges when applied to spatially irregular sensor networks such as those formed by weather stations. In this work, we adopt a graph signal processing perspective and model advection-diffusion particles as signals on a graph to capture the dynamics of these processes. We introduce a Physics-Informed Graph Neural Network (PING) for forecasting future advection-diffusion particle concentrations on irregular grids. The model incorporates a discretized advection-diffusion equation as a soft constraint in the loss function to guide learning toward physically consistent solutions. This model is on par with state of the art models on synthetic and real transport phenomena datasets, including sea surface temperature and cloud index datasets. Furthermore, the PING model is successfully coupled with models for forecasting PV power production. This hybrid approach leverages data fusion from ground-based sensors at PV stations and satellite images with cloud concentration to improve the accuracy of intra-day PV power production.

infographic.key_insight: PING embeds advection–diffusion physics in a graph neural network to forecast transport dynamics on irregular sensor networks and improve solar power forecasting.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More accurate intra-day photovoltaic power forecasts can support grid integration of solar generation.
method: Represent transported particle concentrations as signals on a graph.
Use a discretized advection–diffusion equation as a soft constraint in the training loss.
Couple PING with PV forecasting models using ground-sensor and satellite cloud data.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports performance on par with state-of-the-art models across synthetic and real transport datasets, including sea surface temperature and cloud index data, plus improved intra-day PV forecasts.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative PV forecasting gains, and a soft physics constraint does not guarantee physically consistent predictions.
infographic.paper_title: PING: physics informed graph neural network for advection-diffusion processes with applications to solar power forecasting

title: The Utility of Physics-Informed Machine Learning in Solar Power Production Forecasting
authors: Peter Pavlík, Franz M. Rohrhofer, Bernhard C. Geiger
abstract: Physics-informed machine learning (PIML) and hybrid modeling have attracted significant attention as approaches for combining physical knowledge with the flexibility of deep learning. In this work, we investigate whether these approaches deliver their commonly claimed benefits for large-scale photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting. We develop two hybrid forecasting architectures that integrate the ADR physical PV efficiency model with the TSMixer neural forecasting architecture through feature augmentation and residual learning. The proposed models are evaluated on a dataset comprising over 3 million samples from 3,713 PV installations across 33 European countries. We assess convergence speed, forecasting accuracy, transferability across geographical regions, and data efficiency. Although the physics-informed models seem to exhibit slightly faster convergence during training, they do not achieve consistent improvements in test-set accuracy, generalization, or performance under limited training data compared to the purely data-driven baseline. These findings suggest that, for modern deep forecasting architectures trained on large datasets, explicitly incorporating the ADR physical model provides limited practical benefit for day-ahead PV forecasting.

infographic.key_insight: Adding ADR-based physics to TSMixer provides limited practical benefit for day-ahead photovoltaic power forecasting compared with the purely data-driven baseline.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For large-scale PV forecasting, added physics-model complexity may not yield consistent accuracy, geographic transferability, or data-efficiency gains.
method: Combine the ADR physical PV efficiency model with TSMixer.
Test hybrid architectures using feature augmentation and residual learning.
Compare convergence, accuracy, geographic transferability, and limited-data performance.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation used over 3 million samples from 3,713 PV installations across 33 European countries; hybrids appeared to converge slightly faster but showed no consistent test-performance improvements.
infographic.watch_item: The findings concern ADR–TSMixer hybrids for day-ahead forecasting and should not be generalized to all physics-informed models or solar-cell design tasks.
infographic.paper_title: The Utility of Physics-Informed Machine Learning in Solar Power Production Forecasting

title: VerifiedLab: Harnessing Knowns for Unknowns
authors: Yu Yao, Jiayi Dong, Yang Yang, Shuiwang Ji, Ju Li
abstract: Across human history, knowledge has undergone several transitions, from orality to writing and then to digital archives. At each transition, humans established new conventions to preserve knowledge for the new era. Nowadays, as research agents are increasingly deployed for laboratory experiments, knowledge is crossing another boundary: from records written for humans to those for machines. In this work, we introduce VerifiedLab, a multi-agent harness framework for this human-to-machine transition of knowledge. VerifiedLab transforms research output from passive artifacts into active systems that accelerate downstream use, adoption and prediction of future trends. In VerifiedLab, a team of AI scientists with distinct roles reasons over records verified field by field: a principal investigator plans, a librarian computes the evidence directly from the records, specialists draft, and a gate and a critic check each claim against the measured reliability of its data before the harness decides whether to release or withhold it. We demonstrate the efficacy of VerifiedLab through extensive experiments on perovskite solar cells: VerifiedLab recovers known physical trends, anticipates devices reported a year later, and lets AI scientists inherit the literature together with a measure of how far it can be trusted. By scaling the inference-time verification compute, VerifiedLab introduces a new pathway for knowledge dissemination and machine harness for AI co-scientists.

infographic.key_insight: VerifiedLab turns research records into evidence-checked knowledge that AI scientists can use to analyze and predict perovskite solar cell performance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could support solar cell research by linking AI-generated claims to verified records and data reliability before releasing results.
method: Verify research records field by field.
Assign AI agents to planning, evidence computation, and drafting.
Use gate and critic agents to check claims and decide whether to release or withhold them.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports extensive perovskite solar cell experiments that recover known physical trends and anticipate devices reported a year later, but provides no quantitative metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Practical adoption depends on the quality of record verification and the computational cost of inference-time checks.
infographic.paper_title: VerifiedLab: Harnessing Knowns for Unknowns

title: Virtual-Alloy Physics-Aware Semantic System for extrapolative prediction of perovskite solar cells
authors: Qiwei Han, Chi Zhou
abstract: Existing machine-learning models for perovskite solar cells struggle to predict devices made from new materials. Most treat device layers as arbitrary categorical labels and represent perovskite absorbers either through featureless composition vectors or through rigid crystal graphs that require a pre-solved unit cell. As a result, they cannot generalize to unrecorded alloys or unfamiliar cell architectures. We present the Virtual-Alloy Physics-Aware Semantic System (V-PaSS), an architecture built around the physical continuity of perovskite solid solutions. V-PaSS represents arbitrary mixed-cation, mixed-halide absorbers by interpolating relaxed crystal graphs of 23 pure $ABX_3$ endpoint compounds via Vegard's law with learned bandgap bowing. For the device stack, it couples layer sequence and cell polarity (n-i-p or p-i-n) with interfacial band offsets and encodes chemical descriptions with a scientific language model. Evaluated under an institution-grouped protocol where test devices come exclusively from unseen laboratories, an untuned default configuration of V-PaSS achieves the lowest error among fourteen tested models (2.861% MAE, a 5.2% relative reduction over a gradient-boosted baseline at 3.017%, and outperforming the best tuned benchmark at 2.912%). V-PaSS pulls furthest ahead where test devices differ most from training: reducing error by 15.7-19.0% on unseen absorber alloys, by 16.1% on mixed absorbers from new laboratories, and widening its lead over the baseline by 3.6$\times$ on devices with unobserved transport layers. Combined with tree ensembles, V-PaSS sets a new state of the art across all five benchmark splits.

infographic.key_insight: V-PaSS improves prediction for unfamiliar perovskite solar cells by representing absorber alloys and device stacks through physically informed, chemically meaningful features.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could support screening of new absorber compositions and transport-layer combinations without requiring a pre-solved crystal structure for every alloy.
method: Interpolate relaxed crystal graphs from 23 pure ABX₃ endpoints using Vegard’s law and learned bandgap bowing.
Encode layer sequence, cell polarity, and interfacial band offsets.
Represent chemical descriptions with a scientific language model.
infographic.evidence_signal: On institution-grouped tests with unseen laboratories, untuned V-PaSS achieved 2.861% MAE versus 3.017% for a gradient-boosted baseline, with reported error reductions of 15.7–19.0% on unseen absorber alloys.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization beyond the 23-endpoint representation and the reported benchmark distributions remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Virtual-Alloy Physics-Aware Semantic System for extrapolative prediction of perovskite solar cells
